question: For the paper's simplified autoregressive Transformer class, which finite single-token-label languages can be exactly memorized with and without a generated chain of thought, how many bounded-precision parameters are required, and do either interface or CoT overcome fixed-architecture limits on unbounded-length languages?

key_findings.claim: Without CoT and without positional encoding, finite-language memorization is characterized exactly by a unary-input collision condition.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4.1 states that a finite language S is memorized if and only if any two inputs whose type is the same singleton symbol have the same label; Proposition 4.3 explains necessity because every no-CoT model in the class produces the same classification for all repetitions of one symbol. The constructive upper bound has width O(T), depth O(NLT ceil(L^2 log_2(NLT)/q)), O(T) heads, and O(NLT^4 ceil(L^2 log_2(NLT)/q)) parameters.

key_findings.claim: For the paper's CoT interface, finite memorization also has a necessary-and-sufficient combinatorial characterization, but it is a trace-compatibility result rather than a general computational-expressivity result.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4.4 requires every example to admit a legal continuation z in S_x and requires a common permissible first generated symbol for each unary-input class. When these conditions hold, the construction has width O(T), depth O(NL^2T ceil(L^2 log_2(NLT)/q)), O(T) heads, and O(NL^2T^4 ceil(L^2 log_2(NLT)/q)) parameters. The proof explicitly constructs intermediate prefixes and then applies the no-CoT memorizer to the augmented mapping.

anchors.section: D Proofs of results in Section 4.2

key_findings.claim: The paper's finite LCP example makes CoT and no-CoT look incomparable: unary length-counting subsets favor CoT, whereas non-unary subsets favor no-CoT.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 4.7 says LCP_n cannot be memorized by either interface, LCP_n^{=1} can be memorized only by the CoT interface, and LCP_n^{>1} can be memorized only by the no-CoT interface. These claims follow from the two characterization theorems under the no-position model.

anchors.section: 4.3 CoT and no-CoT-transformers: comparison and more results
E Proofs of results in Section 4.3

key_findings.claim: The apparent case where CoT reduces memorization power is induced by the paper's mandatory-nonempty-CoT protocol and therefore does not establish that permitting optional scratch work can hurt a Transformer.
key_findings.evidence: The no-CoT model returns F(x) directly, but the CoT model must generate at least one non-stop token, condition the same F on the augmented prefix, terminate, and use the final generated token as the label; Remark 3.7 explicitly forbids an empty trace. Thus this CoT hypothesis class does not contain the direct-prediction class. In the LCP_n^{>1} counterexample, required intermediate prefixes collide with longer task inputs. A conventional optional-CoT system could choose zero scratch tokens and emulate direct prediction, so Proposition 4.7's negative direction is interface-specific.

anchors.section: 3 Prerequisite — Transformers with or without CoT
4.3 CoT and no-CoT-transformers: comparison and more results

key_findings.claim: Absolute positional encodings remove the finite no-CoT collision obstruction, while the paper's negative positional result for CoT applies only when every input contains more than one distinct symbol.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 4.8 and Corollary 4.9 construct a bounded-precision no-CoT memorizer for every finite language using position encodings through the maximum length L. Proposition 4.10 says position encoding cannot rescue a CoT-infeasible language only under |typ(x)|>1 for every example. Remark 4.11's broader wording that positional encoding 'has no effect' for CoT omits that hypothesis and the surrounding text acknowledges unary cases can benefit.

anchors.section: 4.3 Position embedding is important for no-CoT-transformer, but not for CoT-transformer

key_findings.claim: Unused vocabulary symbols can serve as collision-free scratch symbols and are sufficient to make every finite language CoT-memorizable under this formalism.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 4.5 gives simple sufficient conditions, including that the set of last input symbols is a proper subset of the vocabulary. Corollary 4.12 strengthens the scratch-symbol observation: if the union of symbols used by inputs is a proper subset of the basic alphabet, a CoT memorizer exists.

anchors.section: 4.3 More basic symbols are important for CoT-transformer

key_findings.claim: Some bounded-precision finite languages require essentially linear parameter count in dataset size for both interfaces, but the advertised optimality is asymptotic under fixed alphabet and precision and N much larger than length.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 5.1 constructs languages of maximum length O(log N) that cannot be memorized below an Omega(N log T / q) parameter threshold. Remark 5.2 combines this existential lower bound with the constructive upper bounds and calls the capacity tilde-Theta(N) when q and T are constants and N is treated as the dominant variable. The upper bounds retain substantial L- and T-dependence, so this is not a uniform linear characterization over all regimes or all datasets.

anchors.section: 5.1 O(N) parameters are necessary and sufficient for memorization

key_findings.claim: With unbounded parameter precision, finite memorization architectures can remove their dependence on maximum sentence length, but bounded precision forces some length dependence even for constant-size languages.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 5.3 gives no-CoT depth O(N) and CoT depth O(N^2) constructions whose architecture does not depend on L when q is infinite. Theorem 5.4 then states that for every fixed bounded-precision architecture bound P, a language of at most ten examples over at most five symbols exists at a sufficiently large length that neither interface can memorize it.

anchors.section: 5.2 The length of sentences affects memorization
F.3.2 Proof of Theorem 5.4 for CoT-transformers

key_findings.claim: A fixed model in the analyzed no-position class cannot memorize a specially selected infinite length-counting sublanguage, even with unbounded parameter precision.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 6.1 takes unions of the increasingly long hard finite constructions and rules out both no-CoT and CoT memorization for corresponding infinite LCP sublanguages. The proof uses convergence of outputs on carefully paired long sequences, not an impossibility result for all LCP formulations or for position-aware Transformers.

anchors.section: 6 Memorization of infinite language is hard

key_findings.claim: The arithmetic impossibility is conditional on a uniform positive logit margin and, for CoT, on a prescribed syntactically valid equality trace; the unconditional fixed-precision claim remains a conjecture.
key_findings.evidence: Definition 6.2 requires confidence at least c on every output step. Proposition 6.3 rules out solving all of Arith_p at any precision under that condition, while allowing each finite Arith_{p,n}. For CoT, 'solve' additionally requires traces x=x_1=...=y stop where each transition performs accurate arithmetic. Conjecture 6.4, not a theorem, is the version without the confidence condition for fixed precision.

anchors.section: F.5.1 Proof of Proposition 6.3 for no-CoT transformers
F.5.2 Proof of Proposition 6.3 for CoT-transformers

key_findings.claim: Calling every computable finite table a 'reasoning dataset' does not make exact interpolation evidence of reasoning algorithms or generalization.
key_findings.evidence: Remark 3.3 labels the studied languages reasoning datasets because they are Turing-computable, while Sections 4 and 5 analyze exact fit on explicitly finite sets. The paper cites prior work noting memorization networks need not generalize, supplies no held-out or length-generalization result, and only treats infinite algorithmic behavior through narrow negative constructions. The finite theorems therefore support statements about interpolation capacity, not about learning or executing an unknown reasoning procedure out of distribution.

anchors.section: 6 Memorization of infinite language is hard

key_findings.claim: The practical conclusion that CoT may have little effect on hard problems without explicit algorithms is not empirically tested and is materially broader than the formal results.
key_findings.evidence: The conclusion acknowledges that there are no experiments and that the model omits LayerNorm, positional encodings in most results, and multi-token labels. The theorems concern constructed exact-memorization languages under fixed decimal precision and a particular CoT protocol, so they do not isolate CoT effects in trained modern LLMs.

method.core_idea: Define exact memorization for one shared decoder-only Transformer under two output protocols—direct classification and mandatory autoregressive intermediate generation—and reduce both protocols to consistency of labels over causal-prefix equivalence classes. Construct matching upper bounds and adversarial counting/convergence lower bounds.
method.mechanism: Symbols receive learned embeddings and pass through causal softmax-attention/ReLU layers; the last-row logits select one symbol or stop. For finite upper bounds, attention-derived position values encode symbol-occurrence patterns, ReLU networks separate the finitely many encodings, and an output map recalls the target. CoT memorization first chooses legal augmented traces whose intermediate prefixes do not demand inconsistent next symbols and memorizes the resulting prefix-to-next-token table. Finite parameter lower bounds count how many fixed-decimal parameter settings can label a family of languages; length and infinite-language lower bounds construct long sequences whose last-row representations converge although required labels or traces differ.
assumptions: Inputs and labels are sequences over a fixed finite alphabet, and every ground-truth label is exactly one token; a separate stop symbol is not allowed in inputs or labels.
The CoT protocol must emit a finite, nonempty sequence and returns its final non-stop token as the label; it cannot choose the direct zero-step path.
The same autoregressive function F maps every task input and every intermediate augmented prefix to a next symbol, creating prefix-consistency constraints.
Most theorems omit positional encoding; Proposition 4.8 adds learned encodings only for the first L positions, and Proposition 4.10 has a non-unary-input hypothesis.
The analyzed Transformer omits LayerNorm and uses causal softmax attention, ReLU feed-forward layers, learned symbol embeddings, a last-row linear output, and optional residual matrices.
Finite precision q means every parameter is a q-digit decimal of magnitude at most 10^q; q=infinity removes this restriction but still leaves a fixed finite architecture.
Upper bounds are existence constructions computable in time polynomial in N, T, L, and q; they do not claim gradient-based learnability, robustness, or practical architectural size.
Infinite arithmetic 'solving' requires a uniform positive logit margin and, for CoT, a restricted sequence of valid equality-preserving arithmetic reductions.
The infinite-language negative results remain within the paper's largely position-free architecture and do not quantify over modern normalized, position-aware LLMs.

techniques.role: Turns exact autoregressive memorization into the requirement that identical prefixes never demand inconsistent next-token outputs.
Uses softmax attention on symbol-indicator embeddings to build bounded-precision signatures of occurrence patterns and sequence positions for finite-set separation.
Implements the final finite lookup from separated scalar/vector encodings to next symbols or labels.
Reduces CoT memorization to a no-CoT lookup over input and intermediate prefixes after selecting collision-compatible traces.
Counts bounded-precision parameter assignments versus possible labelings to construct a language requiring Omega(N log T/q) parameters.
Shows fixed causal attention/FNN representations for paired patterned sequences become arbitrarily close as length grows, contradicting different required labels or a fixed confidence margin.
Appendix A folds residual linear maps into adjacent attention/FNN parameters to argue they reduce parameter cost but not expressivity in this architecture.

evaluations.setting: Arbitrary finite single-token-label language, no CoT, bounded decimal precision, and no positional encoding
evaluations.metric: Necessary-and-sufficient exact-memorization condition and constructive parameter upper bound
evaluations.result: Memorizable exactly iff repeated inputs made from the same single symbol never carry different labels; a construction uses O(NLT^4 ceil(L^2 log_2(NLT)/q)) parameters.
evaluations.baseline: Direct last-token classification by the same simplified Transformer class without scratch generation

evaluations.setting: Arbitrary finite single-token-label language under mandatory nonempty CoT
evaluations.metric: Necessary-and-sufficient trace-feasibility condition and constructive parameter upper bound
evaluations.result: Memorizable exactly iff every example has a legal collision-compatible continuation and unary classes share an allowable first generated symbol; a construction uses O(NL^2T^4 ceil(L^2 log_2(NLT)/q)) parameters.
evaluations.baseline: The paper's no-CoT characterization on the same language

evaluations.setting: Finite length-calculation problem LCP_n without positional encodings
evaluations.metric: Exact memorization of the full, unary-only, and non-unary subsets
evaluations.result: Neither interface memorizes full LCP_n; only mandatory CoT memorizes LCP_n^{=1}, and only no-CoT memorizes LCP_n^{>1}.
evaluations.baseline: CoT versus no-CoT protocols with the same finite-precision architecture

evaluations.setting: Finite languages with learned positional encodings through maximum length L
evaluations.metric: Existence of an exact no-CoT memorizer
evaluations.result: Every finite language becomes no-CoT-memorizable at bounded precision; the corresponding CoT non-rescue theorem covers only languages whose inputs are all non-unary.
evaluations.baseline: Position-free finite-language conditions in Theorems 4.1 and 4.4

evaluations.setting: Worst-case bounded-precision finite languages of N examples and maximum length O(log N)
evaluations.result: Some language satisfying the respective feasibility condition cannot be memorized by either interface below Omega(N log T/q) parameters.
evaluations.baseline: Constructive upper bounds, which become tilde-linear in N only when q and T are fixed and N dominates L

evaluations.setting: At most ten length-counting examples over at most five symbols, with sequence length allowed to increase
evaluations.metric: Exact memorization by any architecture whose width, depth, and head count are all at most fixed P
evaluations.result: For every bounded precision q and architecture cap P, some sufficiently long finite sublanguage defeats both protocols.
evaluations.baseline: Unbounded-precision finite constructions whose architecture can be independent of maximum length

evaluations.setting: Constructed infinite sublanguages of the length-counting problem
evaluations.metric: Exact memorization by any fixed model in the analyzed class
evaluations.result: Neither interface memorizes the selected infinite sublanguage, even when parameter precision is unrestricted.
evaluations.baseline: Every compatible finite truncation has an existence construction when architecture may grow

evaluations.setting: Modular arithmetic language Arith_p at finite and unbounded expression length
evaluations.metric: Correct label or prescribed correct CoT with uniform confidence c>0
evaluations.result: Every finite-length truncation is solvable by an existence construction, but no fixed analyzed model solves the infinite language with a uniform positive confidence margin.
evaluations.baseline: No-CoT versus mandatory valid-equality-trace CoT; the no-margin fixed-precision statement is left as Conjecture 6.4

evaluations.metric: Experiments, learned-model behavior, held-out accuracy, or length generalization
evaluations.baseline: Not applicable; all claimed results are formal existence or impossibility statements

limitations: The CoT class is not a superset of direct prediction because a nonempty trace is mandatory; this design choice is central to the claimed incomparability.
Only single-token labels are modeled, excluding free-form answers and most realistic sequence-generation supervision.
LayerNorm is omitted, and positional encoding is omitted in most results; conclusions do not directly transfer to standard modern decoder-only LLMs.
Finite-language theorems establish exact interpolation existence, not trainability, data efficiency, robustness, compositional execution, or out-of-distribution generalization.
The constructed memorization networks can have very large depth/head/width polynomials and are not practical architectures.
The tilde-Theta(N) capacity summary suppresses substantial length/alphabet factors and depends on fixed precision and alphabet with N much larger than L.
The infinite arithmetic theorem needs a uniform positive margin, and the CoT version additionally imposes one narrow valid trace grammar; the broader claim is only conjectured.
No experiments test the paper's practical interpretations, and no comparison controls for training procedure, optional CoT, positional encoding, normalization, or finite numerical arithmetic.

The appendix alternates labels for the query/key/value projection matrices in some displayed attention formulas relative to Section 3, which complicates line-by-line verification even though the convergence and construction arguments appear invariant to renaming.
The work studies fixed finite vocabularies and learned embeddings rather than tokenization, natural-language semantics, or externally verifiable reasoning steps.
failure_modes: Two unary inputs of different lengths but the same repeated symbol require different direct labels: position-free no-CoT representations collide.
A mandatory CoT continuation makes an augmented prefix identical to another longer task input that requires a different output: no shared autoregressive F can satisfy both.
Every input-ending symbol is already used and no collision-free scratch symbol exists: the simple sufficient CoT construction fails.
A positional-encoding conclusion is applied to unary-input CoT datasets even though Proposition 4.10 explicitly assumes all inputs contain more than one distinct symbol.
Dataset length grows while bounded precision and width/depth/head count remain fixed: paired long-sequence representations converge and labels become inseparable.
A finite lookup result is interpreted as an algorithmic reasoning or length-generalization result despite there being no learned or held-out evaluation.
The arithmetic output margin shrinks toward zero on longer expressions: exact argmax may remain formally possible, but the paper's uniform-confidence solving criterion fails.
The direct model is compared with a forced-generation model rather than an optional scratchpad model: an interface restriction is mistaken for an inherent downside of allowing CoT.
Position-aware or normalized Transformer behavior is inferred from a position-free, LayerNorm-free architecture outside the theorem hypotheses.
reusable_insights: For any autoregressive memorization problem, explicitly construct the prefix-to-next-token table; contradictory targets on an identical prefix are an architecture-independent obstruction.
When comparing scratchpad and direct interfaces, require the scratchpad class to contain a zero-step or immediate-answer path if the scientific question is whether optional reasoning helps.

Separate finite interpolation, bounded-length algorithm simulation, and unbounded-length computation; they require different proof obligations and should not share the label 'reasoning capability' without qualification.
Unused output symbols can function as private control states that avoid collisions with task inputs, analogous to scratch alphabets in automata or delimiters in prompting.
Precision, parameter magnitude, architecture size, and sequence length should be tracked jointly; an architecture independent of length may hide information in unbounded-precision weights.
Adversarial long-sequence convergence is a useful template for proving limits of normalized attention averages when a fixed network must preserve counting information indefinitely.
State theorem scope beside prose conclusions, especially for positional encodings and confidence assumptions, to prevent a restricted proposition from becoming an unconditional narrative claim.
open_questions: Does an optional-CoT hypothesis class that strictly contains direct prediction ever require fewer bounded-precision parameters for exact finite memorization, and can it ever be less expressive under a fair containment definition?
How do the characterizations change for multi-token outputs, separate answer and scratch vocabularies, explicit answer delimiters, or verifier-constrained traces?
Do analogous lower bounds hold for standard pre-norm or post-norm Transformers with rotary/relative positional encodings and finite machine arithmetic?
Can Arith_p be ruled out for fixed-precision CoT and no-CoT Transformers without a uniform confidence condition, resolving Conjecture 6.4?
Which finite memorization constructions are learnable by gradient descent with polynomial samples and optimization time rather than merely representable?
Can a capacity measure separate rote table storage from reusable algorithmic state transitions and predict length generalization?
How tight are the dependencies on L, T, and q between the constructive upper bounds and the counting/convergence lower bounds?
Would independent position indices or a dedicated scratch channel eliminate the prefix collisions that drive Theorem 4.4 and Proposition 4.7?

competitive_landscape.title: The Expressive Power of Transformers with Chain of Thought
competitive_landscape.relationship: A direct theoretical analysis of how autoregressive scratchpad length changes decoder-only Transformer expressivity.
competitive_landscape.difference: It characterizes language/complexity classes as the number of CoT steps grows, including regular-language and polynomial-time regimes, whereas this paper characterizes exact finite-table memorization under mandatory nonempty traces and gives separate infinite counterexamples.

competitive_landscape.title: Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems
competitive_landscape.relationship: Studies constant-depth/constant-precision decoder-only Transformers and the serial computation enabled by T generated CoT steps.
competitive_landscape.difference: It proves constructive circuit-simulation gains and reports synthetic task experiments; this paper instead asks whether a particular forced-CoT protocol changes exact memorization and emphasizes worst-case non-gains.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Revealing the Mystery behind Chain of Thought: A Theoretical Perspective
competitive_landscape.relationship: Uses circuit complexity to compare immediate answers with autoregressive CoT on arithmetic, equations, and dynamic programming.
competitive_landscape.difference: It establishes constant-size CoT constructions for algorithmic tasks and empirical learnability, while the focal paper treats finite exact interpolation and conditional infinite impossibility in a different simplified model.

competitive_landscape.title: Ehrenfeucht-Haussler Rank and Chain of Thought
competitive_landscape.relationship: Gives a structural measure of the minimum CoT steps needed by a single-layer hard-attention Transformer for Boolean functions.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its resource is trace length and its model is hard attention over functions such as composition and kth-occurrence; the focal paper's resources are fixed-decimal parameters and architecture size for softmax-attention memorization.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Optimal Memorization Capacity of Transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Provides close parameter-count bounds for Transformer memorization in next-token and sequence-to-sequence settings.
competitive_landscape.difference: It obtains tilde-O(sqrt(N)) next-token memorization under data/separation and precision regimes and analyzes parameter sharing; the focal paper insists on fixed decimal precision for arbitrary-language worst cases and derives an existential near-linear lower bound.

competitive_landscape.title: Next-token prediction capacity: general upper bounds and a lower bound for transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Quantifies how many distinct contexts a decoder-only Transformer can interpolate with arbitrary or empirical next-token distributions.
competitive_landscape.difference: It studies distribution interpolation and a one-layer injectivity construction, whereas the focal paper studies deterministic single-token labels, a mandatory CoT decoding protocol, and bounded-decimal worst cases.

competitive_landscape.title: Memorization Capacity of Multi-Head Attention in Transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Analyzes the number of example sequences memorized by multi-head attention as a function of heads, dimension, and context size.
competitive_landscape.difference: It assumes linear independence/separation and validates synthetic fitting; the focal paper covers autoregressive direct/CoT consistency, fixed decimal precision, and adversarial languages rather than favorable-position inputs.

competitive_landscape.title: How Numerical Precision Affects Arithmetical Reasoning Capabilities of LLMs
competitive_landscape.relationship: Directly studies how numerical precision changes Transformer arithmetic expressivity and includes precision-controlled experiments.
competitive_landscape.difference: It frames low- versus standard-precision circuit-style arithmetic computation, while the focal paper defines q-digit bounded parameters, proves finite memorization/length effects, and uses a uniform-margin limit for infinite modular arithmetic.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first fixed-precision autoregressive memorization characterization comparing CoT and no-CoT Transformers, near-linear worst-case parameter necessity/sufficiency, length-dependent finite lower bounds, and infinite-language limitations showing that CoT does not always add power.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Theorems 4.1 and 4.4 give interface-specific necessary-and-sufficient finite conditions; Theorem 5.1 supplies a bounded-precision counting lower bound; Theorem 5.4 and Propositions 6.1/6.3 extend the analysis to growing and unbounded length.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The prefix-consistency characterization and joint precision/length lower-bound program are useful and relatively distinctive. The broad 'CoT can hurt or fail to help reasoning' interpretation is much less novel or secure: positive expressivity and precision results already exist, and the focal incomparability depends on forcing at least one scratch token so that its CoT class excludes direct prediction. Its strongest defensible novelty is therefore a characterization of one constrained autoregressive memorization interface, not a general verdict on optional chain-of-thought reasoning.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text audit covered all 36 indexed pages, including every displayed theorem/equation, the complete Sections 1–7, references on pages 10–12, Appendices A–F and their proofs on pages 13–35, and the Impact Statement on page 36. The paper contains no figures, tables, experiments, or empirical baselines. The official arXiv submission history and API were checked on 2026-08-23: the latest and only revision is arXiv:2511.01190v1. The versioned official PDF (PDF 1.7; 36 pages; every page 612 x 792 points) was independently downloaded from export.arxiv.org and matched the indexed PDF SHA-256 exactly; the cached page-marked text matched the indexed text SHA-256 and had text on 36/36 pages. All substantive claims above use PDF page anchors. I separately audited theorem hypotheses, construction/lower-bound regimes, proof endpoints, negative results, limitations, and prose-to-theorem scope. Minor source-quality concerns include frequent typographical errors and inconsistent Q/K/V projection labels between the main architecture formula and some appendix formulas; I found no resulting contradiction that changes a stated theorem, but these notational switches reduce proof auditability. Competitor metadata was checked against the official arXiv API and versioned abstract pages on 2026-08-23; every landscape entry records the current revision observed then.
